grammar.md:
**Twenty-four letters.** Greek is written with an alphabet the Greeks adapted from the Phoenicians around 800 BC. Athenian children learned it in this order, and the order still matters for dictionaries: α β γ δ ε ζ η θ ι κ λ μ ν ξ ο π ρ σ τ υ φ χ ψ ω.

**Capitals and small letters.** Athenians of 431 BC wrote only capitals, with no spaces: ΟΑΡΙΣΤΩΝΚΕΡΑΜΕΥΣΕΣΤΙΝ. The small letters were invented a thousand years later by Byzantine scribes. Modern printed texts use capitals only for names and, in some editions, the start of a paragraph.

**How they sounded (Classical Attic, c. 400 BC).** This course uses the reconstructed pronunciation of Athens in the age of Socrates, not Modern Greek and not the 'Erasmian' school habit. The letters that trip up newcomers:

| letter | sound | note |
|---|---|---|
| β | *b* as in *big* | not *v* |
| γ | *g* as in *go* | before κ, γ, χ, ξ it is *ng* as in *sing* |
| δ | *d* | not *th* |
| ζ | *zd* | as in *wisdom* |
| θ | *t* with a puff of air | like *t* in *top*, not English *th* |
| φ | *p* with a puff of air | like *p* in *pot*, not *f* |
| χ | *k* with a puff of air | like *k* in *kit*, not *ch* |
| σ | *s* | ς at the end of a word |
| ξ | *ks* | |
| ψ | *ps* | |

The vowels come next lesson. Listen to the audio for every word you meet; the voice uses these values throughout.

exercises.explain: ῥῶ = Ρ ρ. It looks like a Latin P but is our R.
νῦ = Ν ν. It looks like a Latin v but is our N; υ (ὖ ψιλόν) is the vowel.
ἦτα = Η η, a long *e*. It looks like a Latin n.

culture.title: The oldest Greek writing
culture.md: The **Dipylon oinochoe**, a wine jug found in the Kerameikos and made around 740 BC, carries one of the oldest Greek inscriptions: a line of verse scratched around its shoulder, written right to left in the early Attic alphabet, promising the jug as a prize to the best dancer. Ariston's great-great-grandparents would have seen letters like these. By his own time Athens had schools where boys learned to read from wax tablets and papyrus, and the assembly voted on decrees that were carved in stone and set up on the Acropolis for anyone to read.
